hitchcock.signature: The master of suspense, who planned his films shot by shot and made the audience complicit in looking.

facts.text: Appears in a brief cameo in most of his films.
Shot Rope to look like a single continuous take.
Was nominated five times for the Best Director Oscar and never won.

hitchcock.description: An English director who became Hollywood's most recognisable name. He storyboarded in detail and built scenes on what the viewer knows and the character does not, usually from a single character's point of view.

welles.signature: Reinvented film language at 25 with deep focus, long takes and a fractured story, then spent his career fighting for money and final cut.

facts.text: Citizen Kane was his first feature, shot by Gregg Toland.
Touch of Evil opens with a crane shot lasting more than three minutes.
Left several films unfinished; The Other Side of the Wind was completed and released in 2018.

welles.description: A theatre and radio prodigy given unprecedented control over his first film. After Citizen Kane he worked mostly outside the studios, shooting in fragments across Europe whenever money allowed.

ford.signature: Turned Monument Valley into the landscape of American myth and framed people against doorways and horizons.

facts.text: Won four Oscars for directing, still the record.
Worked with John Wayne across more than three decades.
The Searchers opens and closes on a doorway.

ford.description: Directed over a hundred films from the silent era to the 1960s, above all westerns. His compositions are simple and monumental, and his subject is community: its rituals, its outsiders and its myths.

sirk.signature: Hid sharp social criticism inside glossy Technicolor melodramas.

facts.text: Left Germany in 1937 and made his best-known films at Universal in the 1950s.
Retired from Hollywood after Imitation of Life in 1959.
Used mirrors and windows to show characters trapped by appearances.

sirk.description: A German theatre director who fled the Nazis. His 1950s melodramas look like lush women's pictures and work as critiques of American conformity, which is why later directors keep returning to them.

kubrick.signature: A perfectionist who reinvented a different genre with almost every film and controlled every detail.

facts.text: Lit scenes of Barry Lyndon by candlelight, using lenses developed for NASA.
The Shining was among the first features to make extensive use of the Steadicam.
Started out as a photographer for Look magazine.

kubrick.description: An American who settled in England and made thirteen features across nearly every genre. He was known for exhaustive research, technical innovation and dozens of takes.

kurosawa.signature: Brought kinetic editing, weather and moral weight to the action film, and was remade around the world.

facts.text: Rashomon won the Golden Lion in 1951 and opened Western eyes to Japanese cinema.
Seven Samurai was remade as The Magnificent Seven.
Cast Toshiro Mifune in sixteen films.
George Lucas drew on The Hidden Fortress for Star Wars.

kurosawa.description: The Japanese director best known abroad, drawing on Shakespeare, Dostoevsky and the American western. He shot action with several cameras and long lenses and cut it with driving rhythm.

ozu.signature: Filmed family life from a low, fixed camera and found the drama in what goes unsaid.

facts.text: Placed the camera at about the eye level of someone sitting on a tatami mat.
Ignored the 180-degree rule and had actors speak almost into the lens.
Cut to empty rooms and streets between scenes, often called pillow shots.
His gravestone bears a single character, mu, meaning nothingness.

ozu.description: Spent his whole career at the Shochiku studio, refining one subject: the Japanese family as children marry and parents age. Over time he removed camera movement, fades and dissolves until only cuts and stillness remained.

mizoguchi.signature: Told stories of women's suffering in long, flowing takes that keep a respectful distance.

facts.text: Won prizes at Venice three years running, from 1952 to 1954.
Worked by the principle of one scene, one shot.
Much of his early work is lost.

mizoguchi.description: Directed from the early 1920s until his death in 1956, and became known in the West only in his last years. His camera moves like a scroll painting unrolling, keeping its distance from suffering.

bergman.signature: Turned the human face into a landscape and made doubt, faith and marriage his subjects.

facts.text: Worked with cinematographer Sven Nykvist for decades.
Kept a company of actors including Liv Ullmann, Max von Sydow and Bibi Andersson.
Lived and filmed on the island of Fårö.

bergman.description: A Swedish theatre director who wrote almost all his own films. With a small troupe of actors he examined faith, marriage, illness and artistic vanity, often on a bare island.

dreyer.signature: Stripped cinema down to faces, walls and silence in search of the spiritual.

facts.text: The Passion of Joan of Arc is built almost entirely from close-ups of actors wearing no make-up.
Made only fourteen features in a career of almost fifty years.
Ordet won the Golden Lion in 1955.

dreyer.description: A Danish director who made few films, years apart, each with a different style. All share a slow, stripped intensity and a focus on women persecuted for their faith or love.

bresson.signature: Rejected acting altogether: he called his performers models and drained their delivery of expression.

facts.text: Set out his method in the book Notes on the Cinematograph.
Made thirteen features in forty years.
Often shows hands, doors and feet where others would show faces.
Was himself a prisoner of war, an experience behind A Man Escaped.

bresson.description: Developed a system he called the cinematograph, opposed to filmed theatre. He used non-professionals drilled to speak without inflection, and built scenes from fragments of gesture and sound.

tarkovsky.signature: Called filmmaking sculpting in time and filled his long takes with water, fire and memory.

facts.text: Completed only seven features.
Made his last two films in exile from the Soviet Union.
His father, the poet Arseny Tarkovsky, reads his own poems in Mirror.

tarkovsky.description: A Soviet director in constant conflict with the film authorities. His films move at the pace of contemplation, mixing colour and black and white, dream, memory and newsreel.

eisenstein.signature: The theorist of montage, who believed meaning is created when two shots collide.

facts.text: The Odessa Steps sequence in Battleship Potemkin is among the most quoted scenes in film history.
Wrote extensively on film theory.
Never completed his Mexican project, Que Viva Mexico.

eisenstein.description: A Soviet theatre director and engineer who became cinema's first major theorist. He conceived films as arguments made by the collision of shots, and cast by physical type.

vertov.signature: Rejected fiction entirely and used every trick of the camera to show life caught unawares.

facts.text: Born David Kaufman; his adopted name suggests a spinning top.
His wife Elizaveta Svilova edited his films and his brother Mikhail Kaufman shot them.
Another brother, Boris Kaufman, shot On the Waterfront and the films of Jean Vigo.

vertov.description: Founder of the Kino-Eye group, he saw fiction film as a drug and the camera as a machine for seeing truthfully. His films are also catalogues of trick effects.

lang.signature: Built worlds of fate, surveillance and crowds, first in Weimar Germany and then in American film noir.

facts.text: M was his first sound film and identifies its killer by a whistled tune.
Metropolis set the template for the cinematic city of the future.
Left Germany in 1933 and made over twenty films in Hollywood.

lang.description: The leading director of Weimar Germany, where he made monumental silent films and the first great sound thriller. In Hollywood after 1934 he turned his geometry and fatalism into film noir.

murnau.signature: Freed the camera to move and told stories almost without intertitles.

facts.text: The Last Laugh has only one intertitle.
Sunrise won the award for Unique and Artistic Picture at the first Academy Awards.
Died in a car accident in 1931, aged 42.

murnau.description: A German director of the silent era who made the camera mobile and expressive. He went to Hollywood in 1926, made Sunrise for Fox, and died just before the premiere of his last film.

renoir.signature: A humanist who staged life in depth, so the frame feels open on all sides.

facts.text: Son of the painter Pierre-Auguste Renoir.
The Rules of the Game was booed, cut and banned on release, then restored in 1959.
The line that everyone has their reasons comes from The Rules of the Game.

renoir.description: The son of the Impressionist painter. His 1930s films mix comedy and tragedy and let actors move freely through deep, open spaces; the New Wave critics called him the patron of their cinema.

rossellini.signature: Took the camera into the ruined streets of postwar Italy and made a new realism out of necessity.

facts.text: Rome, Open City was shot months after the German occupation ended, on scavenged film stock.
His films with Ingrid Bergman, such as Journey to Italy, pointed the way to modern art cinema.
Spent his later career making historical films for television.

rossellini.description: His war trilogy, shot in the rubble with whatever film stock could be found, launched neorealism. He then moved toward spare studies of marriage and belief, and finally to teaching history on television.

fellini.signature: Began in neorealism and ended in a circus of memory, dreams and spectacle that gave us the word Felliniesque.

facts.text: Won four Oscars for Best Foreign Language Film.
The word paparazzi comes from a character in La Dolce Vita.
Worked with composer Nino Rota on almost all his films.
Shot mainly at Cinecittà, in Studio 5.

fellini.description: A caricaturist and gag writer from Rimini who started in neorealism. From La Dolce Vita onward his films became autobiographical spectacles shot on huge sets.

antonioni.signature: Made alienation visible through architecture, empty space and stories that refuse to resolve.

facts.text: L'Avventura was jeered at Cannes in 1960 and then given a jury prize.
The last minutes of L'Eclisse show a street corner where the lovers fail to appear.
Had trees and grass painted for Red Desert, his first colour film.

antonioni.description: Began in neorealist documentary and turned to the emotional lives of the wealthy. His stories dissolve mid-way while the camera lingers on walls, streets and empty landscapes.

godard.signature: Broke every rule of film grammar and then spent sixty years asking what cinema is.

facts.text: Wrote criticism for Cahiers du cinéma before directing.
Breathless was shot on location without sync sound by Raoul Coutard.
Made a run of films with Anna Karina in the 1960s.
Histoire(s) du cinéma is his eight-part video essay on film history.

godard.description: A Swiss-French critic who became the most radical of the New Wave directors. Each phase of his career, from pop collage to militant essay to video, reinvented how sound, image and text relate.

truffaut.signature: The warmest of the New Wave directors, who followed one character, Antoine Doinel, across twenty years.

facts.text: Jean-Pierre Léaud played Doinel in five films, starting at fourteen.
As a critic he attacked French quality cinema and argued for the director as author.
The 400 Blows ends on one of cinema's best-known freeze frames.

truffaut.description: A critic rescued from delinquency by André Bazin. His films are lyrical, literate and affectionate toward their characters, and often about children or obsessive love.

varda.signature: Moved freely between fiction, documentary and self-portrait, with a curiosity that never dimmed.

facts.text: Her first film, La Pointe Courte (1955), predates the New Wave and was edited by Alain Resnais.
Cléo from 5 to 7 unfolds in close to real time.
Was married to Jacques Demy.
Received an honorary Oscar in 2017.

varda.description: A photographer who made her first film with no training. She called her method cinécriture, writing in film, and kept inventing forms into her nineties.

resnais.signature: Made time and memory the structure of his films, not just their subject.

facts.text: Worked with novelists as screenwriters, including Marguerite Duras and Alain Robbe-Grillet.
Night and Fog was one of the first documentaries about the Nazi camps.
Began as an editor.

resnais.description: Started with documentaries on art and the camps. His features, written by leading novelists, treat consciousness itself as the setting.

bunuel.signature: A lifelong surrealist who attacked church, bourgeoisie and good taste with a straight face.

facts.text: Made Un Chien Andalou with Salvador Dalí.
Worked for years in Mexico before returning to Europe.
Cast two actresses in the same role in That Obscure Object of Desire.
Wrote his late films with Jean-Claude Carrière.

bunuel.description: A Spaniard who worked in France, Mexico and Spain. His plain, unshowy direction makes his attacks on religion, class and sexual hypocrisy all the more disconcerting.

melville.signature: Remade the American gangster film as a cool, near-wordless ritual of hats, trench coats and codes of honour.

facts.text: Took his name from Herman Melville.
Built his own studio in Paris.
Fought in the French Resistance, the subject of Army of Shadows.
His independent way of working made him a model for the New Wave.

melville.description: Took his pseudonym from his favourite American author and built his own studio. His gangster films strip the genre to gesture and code, and his independence showed the New Wave how to work.

tati.signature: Built comedy out of sound, architecture and crowds, with almost no dialogue and no close-ups.

facts.text: Played his own creation, Monsieur Hulot, in four films.
Built a huge modern city set, nicknamed Tativille, for Playtime; its cost ruined him.
Shot Playtime in 70mm so viewers could choose where to look.

tati.description: A music-hall mime who made only six features. His comedy is democratic: gags happen all over a wide frame, and the viewer has to find them.

ray.signature: Brought Indian cinema to the world with quiet, humane films rooted in Bengali life.

facts.text: Pather Panchali was made over several years with a largely amateur crew.
Composed the music for most of his later films.
Was also an illustrator and author.
Received an honorary Oscar in 1992.

ray.description: A Calcutta commercial artist who taught himself to direct. His films observe Bengali life with patience and economy, and he wrote, scored and designed them himself.

leone.signature: Stretched the western into opera with extreme close-ups, long silences and Ennio Morricone's music.

facts.text: Morricone often wrote the music before shooting, and Leone played it on set.
Made Clint Eastwood a star with the Dollars trilogy.
Directed only seven features.

leone.description: A Roman who reinvented the American western in Spain with Italian money. He alternates huge landscapes with extreme close-ups and stretches time until a duel becomes a ceremony.

cassavetes.signature: The father of American independent film, who paid for raw, actor-driven dramas with his own acting fees.

facts.text: Often shot in his own house.
His wife Gena Rowlands starred in many of his films.
Shadows grew out of improvisation in his acting workshop.

cassavetes.description: A successful actor who financed his own films. He wrote full scripts and then let the actors find the scenes, keeping the camera on faces through long emotional confrontations.

altman.signature: Filled the frame and the soundtrack with people talking at once and let their stories overlap.

facts.text: Recorded actors on separate microphones so he could mix overlapping dialogue.
Nashville follows twenty-four main characters.
Used a slow, drifting zoom as a signature.

altman.description: A television veteran who became the great satirist of 1970s America. He let large casts improvise, recorded them on multiple tracks and roamed among them with the zoom.

scorsese.signature: Combines restless camera movement, rock music and Catholic guilt in stories of men on the edge.

facts.text: Thelma Schoonmaker has edited every one of his features since Raging Bull.
Has made ten features with Robert De Niro.
Founded The Film Foundation to preserve and restore films.

scorsese.description: Grew up in New York's Little Italy and came out of NYU film school. His films study violent, guilt-ridden men with an encyclopaedic knowledge of film history behind every shot.

malick.signature: Makes films like whispered prayers: natural light, a roaming camera and voice-over in place of plot.

facts.text: Studied philosophy and translated Heidegger before turning to film.
Let twenty years pass between Days of Heaven and The Thin Red Line.
Much of Days of Heaven was shot at magic hour.

malick.description: Studied philosophy before making two films in the 1970s and then disappearing for twenty years. His later films are assembled in the edit from roaming footage and whispered voice-overs.

spielberg.signature: The most commercially successful director in history, with an instinct for staging, wonder and suspense.

facts.text: Has worked with composer John Williams since 1974.
Jaws is often credited as the first summer blockbuster.
Often plays a whole scene in one moving shot instead of cutting.

spielberg.description: The defining popular filmmaker of his era. He combines classical staging in long, moving takes with an instinct for awe and suspense, and has alternated entertainments with historical dramas.

lynch.signature: Found dread under the surface of small-town America and made dream logic feel like plot.

facts.text: Trained as a painter.
Spent about five years making Eraserhead.
Designed much of his own sound.
Worked with composer Angelo Badalamenti from Blue Velvet onwards.

lynch.description: A painter who came to film through animation. His films mix small-town innocence with nightmare, and treat sound as seriously as image.

herzog.signature: Chases what he calls ecstatic truth, in jungles, deserts and extreme states of mind.

facts.text: Had a real steamship hauled over a hill for Fitzcarraldo.
Made five films with the volatile actor Klaus Kinski.
Narrates his own documentaries.

herzog.description: A self-taught Bavarian who has filmed on every continent. He treats documentary and fiction as the same pursuit, inventing and staging in search of what he calls ecstatic truth.

fassbinder.signature: Made over forty films in about fifteen years, turning Hollywood melodrama into a critique of West Germany.

facts.text: Died in 1982, aged 37.
Worked with a regular troupe that began in his Munich theatre group.
Berlin Alexanderplatz runs over fifteen hours.

fassbinder.description: The driving force of the New German Cinema. He worked at furious speed with a fixed troupe, applying the forms of Hollywood melodrama to stories of exploitation in West Germany.

akerman.signature: Made time itself the drama, showing domestic routine at full length from a fixed, frontal camera.

facts.text: Made Jeanne Dielman at 25 with a largely female crew.
In 2022 Jeanne Dielman topped the Sight and Sound critics' poll, the first film by a woman to do so.
Her mother, a Holocaust survivor, is a constant presence in her work.

akerman.description: A Belgian director who saw avant-garde film in New York at twenty-one. Her films combine its rigour with European narrative, and return constantly to rooms, routines and her mother.

kiarostami.signature: Blurred the line between fiction and documentary until the distinction stopped mattering.

facts.text: Close-Up restages a real court case with the people involved playing themselves.
Much of Taste of Cherry and Ten takes place inside moving cars.
Began making films at an institute for children's education.

kiarostami.description: Started at an Iranian institute for children's education. His films are deceptively simple journeys that question what is staged and what is real, and leave their endings to the viewer.

almodovar.signature: Mixes melodrama, comedy and noir in saturated colour, with women at the centre.

facts.text: Emerged from La Movida, Madrid's counterculture after Franco.
Has worked repeatedly with Penélope Cruz, Antonio Banderas and Carmen Maura.
Runs his production company, El Deseo, with his brother Agustín.

almodovar.description: Self-taught, he emerged from Madrid's post-Franco counterculture. His films combine outrageous plots with deep sympathy for their characters, most of them women.

haneke.signature: A cold, precise moralist who makes viewers ask why they are watching.

facts.text: Remade his own Funny Games shot for shot in English.
Rarely uses music unless it has a source inside the scene.

haneke.description: An Austrian who came from theatre and television. His films confront comfortable audiences with violence they would prefer not to consider, withholding explanation and release.

tarr.signature: Films a bleak, muddy Hungary in black and white, in takes that can last ten minutes.

facts.text: Sátántangó runs over seven hours.
Worked closely with novelist László Krasznahorkai, composer Mihály Víg and editor Ágnes Hranitzky.
Announced his retirement from features after The Turin Horse.

tarr.description: A Hungarian director whose late films, made with the novelist László Krasznahorkai, follow people through mud, wind and rain in intricately choreographed long takes.

kaurismaki.signature: Tells stories of Finnish outsiders with minimal dialogue, stoic faces and old rock and roll.

facts.text: His films rarely run much over ninety minutes.
His brother Mika is also a director.
Prefers to shoot on 35mm film.

kaurismaki.description: Finland's best-known director. His working-class fables are laconic and funny, lit like 1950s melodramas and scored with rock and roll and tango.

jarmusch.signature: The cool minimalist of American independent film, drawn to drifters, strangers and dead time.

facts.text: Often casts musicians, including Tom Waits, John Lurie and Iggy Pop.
Stranger Than Paradise is built from single-shot scenes separated by black.
Studied under Nicholas Ray at NYU.

jarmusch.description: Came out of the New York downtown music scene. His films follow outsiders and foreigners drifting through America, and find comedy in pauses and misunderstandings.

coens.signature: Brothers who write, direct and edit together, blending noir plots with deadpan absurdity.

facts.text: Edited many of their films under the pseudonym Roderick Jaynes.
Made a dozen films with cinematographer Roger Deakins.
Frances McDormand, who is married to Joel, won an Oscar for Fargo.

coens.description: Brothers from Minnesota who long shared writing, directing and editing. Their films are intricate genre exercises about foolish schemes, written in heightened regional speech.

vontrier.signature: A provocateur who sets himself rules and restrictions, then breaks them.

facts.text: Co-wrote the Dogme 95 manifesto with Thomas Vinterberg.
Staged Dogville on a bare soundstage with chalk outlines for houses.

vontrier.description: A Danish director who announces rules and manifestos for each project. His films put suffering heroines through ordeals designed to test the audience as much as the characters.

dardenne.signature: Brothers who follow working-class characters around Seraing, Belgium, with the camera at their shoulder.

facts.text: Began in documentary.
Nearly all their features are set in and around their home town.

dardenne.description: Belgian brothers who made documentaries for twenty years. Their features follow one person through a moral crisis, with the camera inches from the back of the neck.

denis.signature: Tells stories through bodies, skin and rhythm more than through dialogue.

facts.text: Grew up in colonial West Africa, a recurring setting in her films.
Works with cinematographer Agnès Godard and the band Tindersticks.
Assisted Wim Wenders and Jim Jarmusch before directing.

denis.description: Grew up in French colonial Africa and assisted Wenders and Jarmusch. Her films are sensual and elliptical, more interested in bodies and rhythm than in explanation.

wong.signature: Films longing and missed chances in smeared neon, slow motion and pop songs on repeat.

facts.text: Often shoots without a finished script.
Worked with cinematographer Christopher Doyle on his best-known films.
Made Chungking Express quickly during a break from editing Ashes of Time.
Wears sunglasses in nearly every public appearance.

wong.description: A Shanghai-born Hong Kong director. He builds his films in the editing room from months of improvised shooting, turning missed connections into pure mood.

tsai.signature: Films loneliness in long, still takes of people waiting, eating and failing to meet.

facts.text: Has cast Lee Kang-sheng in every one of his features.
Was born in Malaysia and works in Taiwan.
Won the Golden Lion for Vive L'Amour.
Leaking and flooding water runs through many of his films.

tsai.description: A Malaysian-born director working in Taiwan, with the same lead actor in every film. His long static shots of lonely people have a deadpan humour.

koreeda.signature: A patient observer of families, chosen and biological, who began in documentary.

facts.text: Known for natural performances from children, often without giving them a script.
Has also made films in France and South Korea.

koreeda.description: Began in television documentary. His family dramas are gentle on the surface and precise about loss, obligation and what makes people kin.

apichatpong.signature: Makes films in which ghosts, past lives and the jungle sit calmly alongside daily life.

facts.text: Trained as an architect.
Several of his films split into two halves that echo each other.
Goes by the nickname Joe.

apichatpong.description: A Thai director trained as an architect and in Chicago's art school. His films drift between the everyday and the supernatural without marking the border.

reichardt.signature: Makes quiet, small-scale films about people on the margins of the American Northwest.

facts.text: Edits her own films.
Has made four films with Michelle Williams.
Often adapts stories by the Oregon writer Jon Raymond.
Shot Meek's Cutoff in the nearly square Academy ratio.

reichardt.description: Works on small budgets in Oregon and edits her own films. Her stories of people with little money are patient, undramatic and attentive to landscape.

tarantino.signature: A former video-store clerk who rebuilt genre cinema out of dialogue, shuffled chronology and quotation.

facts.text: Has said he will retire after ten films.
Sally Menke edited all his films until her death in 2010.

tarantino.description: A film-obsessed former video-store clerk. He writes long, digressive dialogue scenes and assembles them out of order, borrowing freely from exploitation genres.

wanderson.signature: Builds symmetrical, pastel dollhouse worlds populated by melancholy eccentrics.

facts.text: Worked with cinematographer Robert Yeoman on almost all his live-action features.
Bill Murray appears in most of his films.
The Grand Budapest Hotel changes aspect ratio with each time period.
Has made two stop-motion features.

wanderson.description: A Texan whose style is instantly recognisable: symmetrical frames, lateral tracking shots, pastel palettes and deadpan delivery. Beneath the design are stories of grief and broken families.

pta.signature: Moved from sprawling ensemble films to intense character studies, always with a restless camera.

facts.text: Jonny Greenwood of Radiohead has scored his films since There Will Be Blood.
Shot The Master in 65mm.
Has acted as his own cinematographer on later films.

pta.description: Grew up in the San Fernando Valley, where several of his films are set. He began with sprawling ensembles and turned to intense portraits of obsessive men.

bong.signature: Slides between comedy, horror and social critique inside tightly engineered genre films.

facts.text: Parasite was the first film not in English to win the Oscar for Best Picture.
Draws his own complete storyboards.
Song Kang-ho stars in four of his features.

bong.description: A South Korean director who storyboards every shot. His genre films swerve between comedy and horror and are built on the architecture of class.

park.signature: Tells baroque stories of revenge and desire in meticulous, ornate images.

facts.text: Oldboy won the Grand Prix at Cannes in 2004.
Studied philosophy and worked as a film critic.
Completed his Vengeance trilogy between 2002 and 2005.

park.description: A former critic who studied philosophy. His films are ornate, perverse and exactingly designed, usually about revenge and its futility.

desica.signature: An actor turned director who found heartbreak in the smallest stories of postwar poverty.

facts.text: Worked with the screenwriter Cesare Zavattini.
Cast a factory worker as the father in Bicycle Thieves.
Was a matinee idol as an actor before he directed.

desica.description: A matinee idol who directed with the screenwriter Cesare Zavattini. Their neorealist films find tragedy in a stolen bicycle or an old man's pension.

visconti.signature: An aristocrat and Marxist who began in neorealism and ended in operatic period epics.

facts.text: Ossessione (1943) is often called the first neorealist film.
Also directed opera, including productions with Maria Callas.

visconti.description: A Milanese aristocrat and Communist. His career ran from the proto-neorealism of Ossessione to sumptuous studies of aristocratic decline, staged with an opera director's eye.

rohmer.signature: Made talk the action: his characters explain themselves at length and then do something else.

facts.text: Organised his films in cycles: Six Moral Tales, Comedies and Proverbs, Tales of the Four Seasons.
Edited Cahiers du cinéma before his directing career took off.
Éric Rohmer was a pseudonym for Maurice Schérer.

rohmer.description: The oldest of the New Wave critics. His films are comedies of self-deception in which educated people talk about love and then act against everything they said.

wenders.signature: The poet of the road movie, fascinated by American landscapes and European rootlessness.

facts.text: Worked often with cinematographer Robby Müller.
Also known for documentaries such as Buena Vista Social Club and Pina.

wenders.description: A leading figure of the New German Cinema, obsessed with American music and movies. His road films follow lonely men across landscapes, with Robby Müller's photography.

coppola.signature: Made four landmark films in the 1970s and repeatedly gambled his fortune on personal visions.

facts.text: Founded American Zoetrope with George Lucas.
The troubled shoot of Apocalypse Now is the subject of the documentary Hearts of Darkness.

coppola.description: The first of the film-school generation to succeed in Hollywood. In the 1970s he made four of the decade's defining films and spent the fortune they earned on his own studio.

hou.signature: Recalls Taiwan's past in distant, patient long takes where history happens at the edge of the frame.

facts.text: A City of Sadness won the Golden Lion in 1989.
Several early films draw on his own youth and that of his screenwriters.
Won Best Director at Cannes for The Assassin.

hou.description: The central director of the Taiwan New Wave. He films from a distance in long takes, letting history register in family life and off-screen events.

yang.signature: Mapped modern Taipei as a web of families, offices and reflections in glass.

facts.text: Worked as a computer engineer in the United States before turning to film.
Won Best Director at Cannes for Yi Yi.
A Brighter Summer Day runs nearly four hours.
Died in 2007, having made seven features.

yang.description: A former computer engineer who became the chronicler of Taipei. His films are novelistic in scope, with many characters observed through windows and reflections.

vinterberg.signature: Co-founded Dogme 95 and made its first and most celebrated film.

facts.text: Festen was shot on a consumer video camera.
Won the Oscar for international feature with Another Round.

vinterberg.description: A Danish director who co-wrote the Dogme 95 rules at 26. His films set groups of people against a truth one of them insists on telling.

panahi.signature: Keeps making films in defiance of an official ban, turning the restriction itself into his subject.

facts.text: Was banned from filmmaking in Iran in 2010.
This Is Not a Film was reportedly smuggled out of Iran on a USB stick hidden in a cake.
Taxi, in which he drives a cab around Tehran, won the Golden Bear.

panahi.description: Started as Kiarostami's assistant. Officially banned from filmmaking since 2010, he has kept making films in secret, in his flat, in a taxi and near the border.

chytilova.signature: The most formally radical voice of the Czechoslovak New Wave, anarchic and feminist.

facts.text: Daisies was banned by the Czechoslovak authorities.
Was kept from directing for several years after 1968.
Worked with the designer Ester Krumbachová and the cinematographer Jaroslav Kučera, her husband.

chytilova.description: The first woman to study directing at the Prague film school. Her films are aggressive experiments in montage and colour that mock both consumerism and socialist propriety.

forman.signature: Carried the comic eye of the Czechoslovak New Wave into Hollywood stories of rebels against institutions.

facts.text: Emigrated after the Soviet invasion of 1968.
Won Best Director Oscars for One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest and Amadeus.
The Firemen's Ball was banned in Czechoslovakia.

forman.description: Made comedies with non-actors in Czechoslovakia before emigrating. His American films side with misfits against institutions, from the asylum to the imperial court.

oshima.signature: Attacked Japanese taboos on sex, crime and the state, changing style with every film.

facts.text: In the Realm of the Senses led to an obscenity trial in Japan over the published script.
Left the Shochiku studio after it withdrew his film Night and Fog in Japan.

oshima.description: The leader of the Japanese New Wave. He rejected the humanism of the older masters and attacked taboos around sex, crime and the treatment of Koreans in Japan.

imamura.signature: Said he was interested in the lower part of the human body and the lower part of the social structure.

facts.text: Founded a film school in Yokohama.
Turned to documentary for much of the 1970s.

imamura.description: Ozu's former assistant, who reacted against his refinement. He filmed pimps, bar hostesses and peasants with an anthropologist's curiosity and earthy humour.

leechangdong.signature: A novelist turned director whose slow-burning dramas turn on grief, faith and class.

facts.text: Published fiction before making films.
Served as South Korea's minister of culture.
Burning adapts a short story by Haruki Murakami.

leechangdong.description: A novelist who turned to film in his forties. His slow, morally searching dramas follow people undone by grief or injustice.

loach.signature: Has spent six decades filming working-class Britain with documentary directness and open political anger.

facts.text: Shoots in story order and often withholds the script so actors are surprised.
Has worked with the screenwriter Paul Laverty since the 1990s.

loach.description: Began in BBC television drama in the 1960s. His films are made with social workers' accuracy and often non-professional casts, and are open about their politics.

leigh.signature: Builds his scripts through months of improvisation with the actors before shooting a word.

facts.text: His actors develop their characters separately and learn only what those characters would know.
Has a parallel career in theatre.

leigh.description: Develops each film from nothing through months of improvisation with the cast. The results are precisely scripted tragicomedies of English class and family.

chaplin.signature: Created the Tramp, the most recognised character of the silent era, and mixed slapstick with pathos.

facts.text: Wrote, directed, produced, starred in and scored his films.
Kept making essentially silent films well into the sound era.
Co-founded United Artists in 1919.

chaplin.description: Rose from London poverty to become the most famous man in the world. He controlled every part of his films and shot scenes over and over until the comedy was exact.

keaton.signature: The Great Stone Face, who did his own dangerous stunts and treated the film frame as a gag machine.

facts.text: In Steamboat Bill, Jr. a house front falls around him and he stands where the window lands.
In Sherlock Jr. a projectionist walks into the film he is showing.
Lost creative control after signing with MGM in 1928.

keaton.description: A vaudeville child performer who became the great engineer of silent comedy. His gags are filmed in long, wide shots so the audience can see they are real.

hawks.signature: Mastered almost every Hollywood genre with an invisible style, fast talk and codes of professionalism.

facts.text: His Girl Friday is famous for the speed of its dialogue.
Gave Lauren Bacall her first film role.
Never won a competitive Oscar; received an honorary one late in life.

hawks.description: Made classics in almost every genre without drawing attention to his style. His films are about groups of professionals, and his women talk as fast as his men.

wilder.signature: A writer first, whose cynical wit ran from film noir to farce.

facts.text: Began as a screenwriter in Berlin and fled Germany in 1933.
Won Oscars as producer, director and writer for The Apartment.
Kept a sign in his office asking how Lubitsch would do it.

wilder.description: An Austrian journalist and screenwriter who fled to Hollywood. He always wrote with a partner and directed to protect the script, in dramas and comedies equally cynical about people.

powell.signature: A writer-director partnership, The Archers, who made British cinema's most extravagant colour fantasies.

facts.text: Shared the credit written, produced and directed by.
Worked with cinematographer Jack Cardiff on their Technicolor films.
Powell's solo film Peeping Tom all but ended his career in Britain.

powell.description: The English director Powell and the Hungarian writer Pressburger shared every credit. Their wartime and postwar films are romantic, mystical and visually extravagant, against the realist grain of British cinema.

pasolini.signature: A poet and novelist who filmed the sacred and the scandalous with the same frontal simplicity.

facts.text: Cast his own mother as the older Virgin Mary in The Gospel According to St. Matthew.
Was a major Italian poet and public intellectual before he directed.
Was murdered in 1975, shortly before the release of Salò.

pasolini.description: A poet, novelist and polemicist before he directed. He filmed Roman slum life, the Gospel and medieval tales in a deliberately rough, frontal style he compared to early Renaissance painting.

bertolucci.signature: Combined political history, psychoanalysis and sweeping camera movement.

facts.text: Worked with cinematographer Vittorio Storaro.
The Last Emperor won nine Oscars and was shot inside the Forbidden City.
Published poetry before directing; his father was a poet.

bertolucci.description: A poet's son who was Pasolini's assistant at twenty. His films link sexuality and politics, photographed by Vittorio Storaro in sweeping, colour-coded movements.

chabrol.signature: The New Wave's specialist in murder among the provincial bourgeoisie.

facts.text: Le Beau Serge (1958) is often counted as the first New Wave feature.
Made over fifty features.
Made many films with Stéphane Audran and later with Isabelle Huppert.

chabrol.description: Made the first New Wave feature with an inheritance. He settled into a long series of thrillers that observe bourgeois families with amused detachment.

rivette.signature: Made long, playful films about theatre, conspiracy and performance.

facts.text: Out 1 runs close to thirteen hours.
Edited Cahiers du cinéma in the 1960s.
Often developed his scripts together with his actresses.

rivette.description: The most experimental of the Cahiers critics. His long films, often developed with the actors, imagine Paris as a web of rehearsals and conspiracies.

marker.signature: The great film essayist, who thought aloud about memory, travel and images.

facts.text: La Jetée is composed almost entirely of still photographs.
Avoided interviews and photographs, often sending a picture of a cat instead.
La Jetée inspired the film 12 Monkeys.

marker.description: A writer, photographer and traveller who avoided publicity. His essay films think aloud about memory, politics and images.

demy.signature: Set bittersweet fairy tales in French port towns, in candy colours and often entirely in song.

facts.text: Every line of The Umbrellas of Cherbourg is sung.
Worked with composer Michel Legrand.
Characters from one film reappear in others.
Was married to Agnès Varda.

demy.description: Grew up in Nantes and set his films in French port towns. They look like confectionery and are about chance, absence and lost love.

polanski.signature: A specialist in paranoia and confinement, usually seen through one character's eyes.

facts.text: Survived the Kraków ghetto as a child.
Knife in the Water, his debut, was nominated for the foreign-language Oscar.
Repulsion, Rosemary's Baby and The Tenant are often called his apartment trilogy.

polanski.description: Trained at the Łódź film school and worked in Poland, Britain, Hollywood and France. His films trap characters in rooms and in their own perceptions.

kieslowski.signature: Moved from documentary to metaphysical dramas about chance, coincidence and moral choice.

facts.text: Dekalog is a series of ten films based on the Ten Commandments.
Worked with co-writer Krzysztof Piesiewicz and composer Zbigniew Preisner.
Announced his retirement after Three Colours: Red.

kieslowski.description: A Polish documentarist who came to distrust documentary. His later films are moral fables about chance and connection, tightly designed around colour and music.

angelopoulos.signature: Staged Greek history as slow processions in mist, in takes that travel through time within a single shot.

facts.text: Worked with composer Eleni Karaindrou.
Died in 2012 after being struck by a motorcycle while filming.

angelopoulos.description: A Greek director who told his country's twentieth-century history as myth. His very long takes glide through landscapes while decades pass within a single shot.

mungiu.signature: A leading figure of the Romanian New Wave, known for tense scenes played out in unbroken takes.

facts.text: Typically films each scene in a single shot.
With Fjord in 2026 he became the tenth filmmaker to win the Palme d'Or twice.

mungiu.description: A former journalist and teacher. His films set ordinary Romanians moral traps and watch them in long takes without music.

puiu.signature: Set the template for the Romanian New Wave with long, darkly comic dramas that unfold in near real time.

facts.text: The Death of Mr. Lazarescu won the Un Certain Regard prize at Cannes in 2005.
Trained as a painter.

puiu.description: A painter who started the Romanian New Wave. His films follow people through hospitals and family gatherings in near real time, with grim humour.

depalma.signature: A virtuoso of the set piece, devoted to split screens, long takes and Hitchcock.

facts.text: Favours the split-diopter lens, which holds near and far in focus at once.
Belonged to the circle of friends that included Scorsese, Spielberg, Lucas and Coppola.

depalma.description: Part of the film-school generation. He turns thrillers into exercises in pure cinema, with split screens, long tracking shots and open borrowings from Hitchcock.

peckinpah.signature: Changed screen violence with slow motion and rapid intercutting, in elegies for men out of their time.

facts.text: The Wild Bunch contains far more cuts than was usual for its time.
Fought studios over the editing of several of his films.

peckinpah.description: A television western writer who became the genre's elegist. His films are about ageing men with outdated codes, and their violence is drawn out in slow motion.

spikelee.signature: A confrontational, stylish chronicler of Black American life and of New York.

facts.text: His signature double-dolly shot makes characters appear to float.
Calls his films joints.
Teaches film at NYU.

spikelee.description: Emerged from NYU and Brooklyn in the 1980s. His films are argumentative and stylised, mixing comedy, music and direct address to confront American racism.

linklater.signature: Fascinated by time passing and people talking, often over a single day.

facts.text: Shot Boyhood over twelve years with the same cast.
The Before trilogy revisits the same couple every nine years.
Founded the Austin Film Society.

linklater.description: A self-taught filmmaker from Austin, Texas. He is interested in ordinary time: single days, long conversations and actors ageing across years.

fincher.signature: A perfectionist of dark, precise thrillers, known for demanding dozens of takes.

facts.text: Started out in visual effects and music videos.
Was an early adopter of digital cameras.

fincher.description: Came from visual effects and music videos. His thrillers are controlled to the frame, digitally polished and bleak about institutions and obsession.

nolan.signature: Makes large-scale films built on puzzles of time, favouring film stock and practical effects.

facts.text: Memento tells its story in reverse.
Shoots on IMAX film cameras.
Often writes with his brother Jonathan.

nolan.description: A British-American director who writes most of his own scripts. He builds blockbusters around fractured timelines and prefers film cameras and physical effects.

cronenberg.signature: The originator of body horror, who films mutation and desire with clinical calm.

facts.text: Has made nearly all his films in Canada.
Works with composer Howard Shore.

cronenberg.description: A Canadian who began in low-budget horror. His films treat the body as the place where technology, disease and desire rewrite identity.

zhang.signature: Began as a cinematographer and became China's great colourist.

facts.text: Red Sorghum won the Golden Bear in 1988.
Made a series of films with Gong Li.
Directed the opening ceremony of the 2008 Beijing Olympics.

zhang.description: Trained as a cinematographer in the first class after the Cultural Revolution. His early films used saturated colour to tell stories of oppressed women; later he turned to martial-arts spectacle.

chen.signature: Launched the Fifth Generation and went on to large historical dramas.

facts.text: Yellow Earth (1984) is usually counted as the start of the Fifth Generation.

chen.description: A classmate of Zhang Yimou at the Beijing Film Academy. His debut announced a new Chinese cinema of landscape and silence, and he later made lavish historical dramas.

jia.signature: Records China's upheaval through the people it leaves behind, mixing staged and found reality.

facts.text: Still Life won the Golden Lion in 2006.
Often casts Zhao Tao, his wife.
Many of his films are set in his home province of Shanxi.
Made his first films without official approval.

jia.description: The leading director of China's Sixth Generation. He films provincial towns and migrant workers as the country is rebuilt around them, mixing documentary and fiction.

sembene.signature: Often called the father of African cinema, a novelist who turned to film to reach a wider audience.

facts.text: Black Girl (1966) is often cited as the first feature by a sub-Saharan African director to win international attention.
Worked as a docker in Marseille before becoming a writer.
Studied film in Moscow.
Made films in Wolof as well as French.

sembene.description: A Senegalese novelist who took up film to reach people who could not read. His films criticise colonialism, the new African elite and patriarchal custom.

rocha.signature: The voice of Cinema Novo, who wanted a cinema as violent as the hunger it showed.

facts.text: Wrote the manifesto The Aesthetics of Hunger.
Summed up the movement as a camera in the hand and an idea in the head.
Won Best Director at Cannes for Antonio das Mortes.
Died in 1981, aged 42.

rocha.description: The theorist and leading director of Brazil's Cinema Novo. His films are delirious political allegories set in the drought-stricken backlands.

campion.signature: Films desire and repression from inside her characters, with landscapes that press in on them.

facts.text: Was the first woman to win the Palme d'Or, for The Piano.
Won the Best Director Oscar for The Power of the Dog.
Was the first woman nominated twice for the Best Director Oscar.

campion.description: A New Zealander trained in Australia. Her films centre on women's desire and will, with a strong sense of landscape and touch.

sciamma.signature: Films girlhood, identity and the act of looking with restraint and precision.

facts.text: Portrait of a Lady on Fire has almost no musical score.
Won Best Screenplay at Cannes for Portrait of a Lady on Fire.
Also writes for other directors.

sciamma.description: A French writer-director whose films follow girls and women working out who they are. Her style is spare, with little music and careful attention to looks exchanged.

martel.signature: Builds unease from sound and from what sits just outside the frame.

facts.text: Her first three features are set in Salta, her home region of Argentina.
Has said she thinks about a film's sound before its images.

martel.description: An Argentine director from the northern province of Salta. Her films build a sense of decay and menace from overlapping sound and partial views.

lanthimos.signature: Sets absurd rules for his characters and has them speak in flat, stilted lines.

facts.text: Dogtooth was nominated for the foreign-language Oscar.
Poor Things won the Golden Lion in 2023.
Uses extreme wide-angle and fisheye lenses in his later films.

lanthimos.description: Came out of Greek theatre, video and advertising. His films place characters in closed systems with arbitrary rules and observe them with clinical humour.

ceylan.signature: A former photographer who films Anatolian landscapes and long, searching conversations.

facts.text: Cast himself and his family in his early films.
Often writes with his wife, Ebru Ceylan.

ceylan.description: A Turkish photographer turned director. His films are slow studies of pride and disappointment among provincial men, with long conversations and wide Anatolian landscapes.

kitano.signature: A television comedian who became a director of still, melancholy gangster films punctuated by sudden violence.

facts.text: Is known in Japan as Beat Takeshi.
Hana-bi won the Golden Lion in 1997.
Writes, directs, edits and stars in most of his films.
His own paintings appear in Hana-bi.

kitano.description: One of Japan's most famous comedians, who took over a film when its director fell ill. His crime films alternate long stillness with abrupt violence and childlike play.

ernstlubitsch.signature: Master of sophisticated comedy, famous for the Lubitsch touch: saying the scandalous thing by showing a closed door.
ernstlubitsch.description: Came from Berlin to Hollywood in 1922 and set the standard for witty, adult comedy of manners. His films trust the audience to complete the joke, implying sex and deceit through objects, doors and reaction shots.

facts.text: Billy Wilder kept a sign in his office asking how Lubitsch would do it.
To Be or Not to Be made a comedy about the Nazi occupation of Poland in 1942.

woodyallen.signature: Turned the neurotic New York intellectual into a film genre of its own.
woodyallen.description: A stand-up and gag writer who has made close to a film a year since the 1970s, mixing romantic comedy with borrowings from Bergman and Fellini. Long master shots let his actors talk over and past each other.

facts.text: Annie Hall won Best Picture and has him address the camera directly.
Worked with the cinematographers Gordon Willis and Sven Nykvist.

davidlean.signature: Began with intimate British dramas and became the definition of the widescreen epic.
davidlean.description: A former editor whose cutting is as famous as his vistas. From Brief Encounter to Lawrence of Arabia he kept private emotion at the centre of ever larger canvases.

facts.text: Started as an editor; the cut from a blown-out match to the desert sunrise in Lawrence of Arabia is among the most cited in film.
Shot Lawrence of Arabia in 70mm, largely in the Jordanian desert.

donenkelly.signature: Took the musical out of the theatre and made dance something only a camera could capture.
donenkelly.description: The dancer-choreographer and the young director co-directed three MGM musicals. Their numbers are filmed in long, mobile takes that show the whole body, and Singin' in the Rain turns Hollywood's own conversion to sound into comedy.

facts.text: On the Town (1949) took musical numbers onto real New York locations.
Singin' in the Rain was built around songs written decades earlier by its producer, Arthur Freed.

ridleyscott.signature: A designer of worlds, from the rain-soaked future of Blade Runner to ancient Rome.
ridleyscott.description: Trained as a designer and made hundreds of commercials before turning to features. His films are remembered first for atmosphere: smoke, backlight and densely layered sets.

facts.text: Blade Runner exists in several cuts; the voice-over was removed in later versions.
Directed Apple's '1984' Macintosh commercial.

jeanvigo.signature: Made under three hours of film before dying at 29, and changed French cinema anyway.
jeanvigo.description: The son of an anarchist, he mixed documentary roughness with lyrical fantasy. Zero for Conduct, about a schoolboy revolt, and the barge romance L'Atalante were banned or mutilated on release and rediscovered after the war.

facts.text: Zero for Conduct was banned in France until 1945.
Shot his films with Boris Kaufman, brother of Dziga Vertov.
France's Prix Jean Vigo for young directors is named after him.

maxophuls.signature: The poet of the moving camera, gliding through ballrooms and up staircases after women in love.
maxophuls.description: A German-born director who worked in Germany, France, Hollywood and France again. His elaborate crane and dolly shots circle characters caught between desire and social ritual.

facts.text: La Ronde and Lola Montès are both presented by master-of-ceremonies figures who address the audience.
Lola Montès was recut by its producers after failing at the box office.

michaelcurtiz.signature: The Warner Bros. workhorse who could direct anything, and directed Casablanca.
michaelcurtiz.description: A Hungarian émigré who made around a hundred Hollywood films in every genre. Fluid camera movement and bold shadows give even routine assignments visual drive.

facts.text: Won the Best Director Oscar for Casablanca.
Made a dozen films with Errol Flynn.

johnhuston.signature: A writer-director of adventures about people undone by their own schemes.
johnhuston.description: Began as a screenwriter and adapted literature throughout his career, from Hammett to Joyce. His stories of doomed quests are told plainly, with close attention to faces and group dynamics.

facts.text: Directed his father Walter to an Oscar in The Treasure of the Sierra Madre and his daughter Anjelica to one in Prizzi's Honor.
The Maltese Falcon, his debut, is often called the first major film noir.
Directed his last film, The Dead, from a wheelchair.

dwgriffith.signature: Consolidated the grammar of narrative film, and used it for one of cinema's most racist works.
dwgriffith.description: Made hundreds of shorts at Biograph, refining close-ups and parallel editing into a storytelling system. The Birth of a Nation glorified the Ku Klux Klan and provoked nationwide protest; Intolerance was his colossal reply to his critics.

facts.text: Intolerance cuts between four stories set in different eras.
Co-founded United Artists with Chaplin, Mary Pickford and Douglas Fairbanks.
The NAACP campaigned against The Birth of a Nation on its release.

frankcapra.signature: Champion of the ordinary citizen against the powerful, in fast-talking populist fables.
frankcapra.description: An Italian immigrant who became Columbia's star director. His comedies move at speed but turn on a moment of despair before the community rallies round the hero.

facts.text: Won three Best Director Oscars in the 1930s.
It's a Wonderful Life flopped on release and became a classic through television repeats.
Made the Why We Fight documentaries during the Second World War.

hayaomiyazaki.signature: Hand-draws worlds of flight, forests and spirits, and children who meet them without fear.
hayaomiyazaki.description: Co-founder of Studio Ghibli, where he storyboards his films himself and lets the story emerge as he draws. His films avoid clear villains and leave room for quiet pauses.

facts.text: Spirited Away won the Oscar for animated feature.
Co-founded Studio Ghibli with Isao Takahata in 1985.
Has announced his retirement several times and returned each time.

nicholasray.signature: The poet of outsiders and troubled youth in 1950s Hollywood.
nicholasray.description: His characters are lonely, violent and tender, framed in bold colour and off-balance CinemaScope compositions. The French New Wave critics treated him as proof that a studio director could be an artist.

facts.text: Godard wrote that the cinema is Nicholas Ray.
Rebel Without a Cause made James Dean an icon.
Later taught film; Jim Jarmusch was his assistant.

vincenteminnelli.signature: MGM's great stylist, who treated colour and decor as the emotions of his characters.
vincenteminnelli.description: A former stage designer who made the studio's most elegant musicals and some of its most intense melodramas. His crane shots sweep through crowded, colour-coded sets.

facts.text: An American in Paris ends with a 17-minute ballet.
Was married to Judy Garland; Liza Minnelli is their daughter.

carolreed.signature: Made postwar Europe look tilted and treacherous.
carolreed.description: A British craftsman whose late-1940s thrillers use real ruined cities, steep shadows and canted framing. Several of his stories are seen through the eyes of a child or an innocent out of his depth.

facts.text: The Third Man is famous for its tilted camera angles and zither score.
Won the Best Director Oscar for the musical Oliver!

leomccarey.signature: Moved between anarchic comedy and tearjerkers, often improvising on set.
leomccarey.description: Learned his craft directing Laurel and Hardy shorts. He worked loosely, sometimes inventing scenes at a piano on the set, and let the actors' timing set the rhythm.

facts.text: Paired Stan Laurel with Oliver Hardy.
Ozu's Tokyo Story was inspired by his Make Way for Tomorrow.
Accepting the Oscar for The Awful Truth, he said he had been given it for the wrong film.

victorfleming.signature: The studio fixer credited with both of 1939's most famous films.
victorfleming.description: A former cameraman and reliable MGM professional who took over The Wizard of Oz and Gone with the Wind from other directors. He is remembered less for a personal style than for bringing huge productions home.

facts.text: Replaced George Cukor on Gone with the Wind.
Won the Best Director Oscar for Gone with the Wind.

prestonsturges.signature: Wrote and directed a burst of the fastest, wittiest American comedies within five years.
prestonsturges.description: The first major Hollywood screenwriter of the sound era to direct his own scripts. His films combine sophisticated verbal comedy with pratfalls and a stock company of character actors.

facts.text: Sold the script of The Great McGinty for a nominal fee in exchange for the chance to direct it.
Sullivan's Travels is about a comedy director who wants to make a serious film called O Brother, Where Art Thou?

eliakazan.signature: Brought Method acting from the stage to the screen.
eliakazan.description: Co-founder of the Actors Studio, he drew raw, psychologically detailed performances from Marlon Brando and James Dean. He pushed Hollywood toward location shooting and social subjects.

facts.text: Directed Brando in A Streetcar Named Desire and On the Waterfront.
Named former colleagues to the House Un-American Activities Committee in 1952, which divided Hollywood for decades.

marcelcarne.signature: Defined French poetic realism: doomed lovers in foggy, studio-built streets.
marcelcarne.description: Worked with the poet Jacques Prévert as screenwriter and the designer Alexandre Trauner. Their films of the late 1930s set fatalistic romances in meticulously constructed sets.

facts.text: Children of Paradise was shot during the German occupation.
The designer Alexandre Trauner and composer Joseph Kosma, both Jewish, worked on it in hiding.

nicolasroeg.signature: Shattered chronology so that past, present and premonition play at once.
nicolasroeg.description: A leading cinematographer before he directed. His editing associates images across time, so a scene can be interrupted by what will happen or what is remembered.

facts.text: Was cinematographer on Truffaut's Fahrenheit 451.
Cast rock stars as leads: Mick Jagger, David Bowie and Art Garfunkel.

gillopontecorvo.signature: Made a staged film about colonial war look like captured newsreel.
gillopontecorvo.description: A former partisan and journalist who made only five features. The Battle of Algiers restaged the Algerian uprising on the real streets with a cast made up almost entirely of non-professionals.

facts.text: The Battle of Algiers was kept off French screens for years.
Its American release carried a notice that it contains not one foot of newsreel.

erichvonstroheim.signature: Hollywood's first great realist and its first great casualty of the studio system.
erichvonstroheim.description: An Austrian émigré who invented an aristocratic past for himself. His obsessive detail and adult cynicism led to huge budgets and battles with producers, and most of his films survive only in cut versions.

facts.text: His original cut of Greed ran around eight hours; the studio reduced it to about two.
Later acted in Renoir's Grand Illusion and Wilder's Sunset Boulevard.

victorerice.signature: Made four features in fifty years, each a hushed study of memory and looking.
victorerice.description: His films approach the silence of Spain after the civil war through children and through light falling into rooms. He works so rarely that each film is an event.

facts.text: The Spirit of the Beehive follows a girl haunted by a screening of Frankenstein.
Released his fourth feature, Close Your Eyes, in 2023, three decades after the third.

claudelanzmann.signature: Told the story of the Holocaust without a single frame of archive footage.
claudelanzmann.description: A journalist and editor of Les Temps modernes. Shoah, more than nine hours long, consists only of present-day testimony from survivors, bystanders and perpetrators, and of the sites as they look now.

facts.text: Spent eleven years making Shoah.
Filmed some former SS men with a hidden camera.

josefvonsternberg.signature: Painted with light and shadow, and made Marlene Dietrich a myth.
josefvonsternberg.description: He treated story as a pretext for texture: veils, nets, smoke and shafts of light fill every layer of the frame. His films with Dietrich are studies in desire and humiliation.

facts.text: Made seven films with Marlene Dietrich, beginning with The Blue Angel.
Often took charge of the lighting himself.

jacquestourneur.signature: Frightened audiences with what he did not show.
jacquestourneur.description: The son of the silent director Maurice Tourneur. In low-budget horror for the producer Val Lewton, and later in film noir, he creates threat through shadow, sound and suggestion.

facts.text: The swimming-pool scene in Cat People is built from shadows and echoes alone.
Out of the Past is a model of the flashback-driven film noir.

josephlmankiewicz.signature: Hollywood's most literate writer-director, who built films out of talk and flashbacks.
josephlmankiewicz.description: His films are witty, word-driven studies of ambition, theatre people and marriage, often told by several narrators in turn.

facts.text: Won Oscars for both writing and directing two years running, for A Letter to Three Wives and All About Eve.
His brother Herman co-wrote Citizen Kane.

sidneylumet.signature: The great director of New York, juries, cops and institutions under pressure.
sidneylumet.description: Came from live television and worked fast, with long rehearsals and few takes. His films test individuals against corrupt or indifferent systems.

facts.text: 12 Angry Men, his first feature, takes place almost entirely in one room.
Wrote the handbook Making Movies.

jeaneustache.signature: Made the definitive film about the hangover after May 1968.
jeaneustache.description: A disciple of the New Wave who pushed its talkiness to an extreme. The Mother and the Whore is more than three and a half hours of confession, seduction and monologue in cafés and bedrooms.

facts.text: The Mother and the Whore runs about 3 hours 40 minutes.
Died in 1981, aged 42.

johncarpenter.signature: Made lean genre films in widescreen, and usually wrote the synthesizer score himself.
johncarpenter.description: A devotee of Howard Hawks who applied classical craft to horror and science fiction on small budgets. His films trap small groups with a threat they barely understand.

facts.text: Composed the Halloween theme himself.
Assault on Precinct 13 reworks Hawks's Rio Bravo.

jamescameron.signature: Pushes film technology forward with every blockbuster.
jamescameron.description: A former truck driver and effects technician who writes his own scripts. His films combine engineering ambition with tightly constructed action.

facts.text: Directed three of the highest-grossing films ever made.
Developed new 3D and performance-capture camera systems for Avatar.

clinteastwood.signature: The western's last star became its most reflective director.
clinteastwood.description: Works quickly and economically, with few takes and low-key lighting. As a director he keeps returning to violence and what it costs the people who use it.

facts.text: Dedicated Unforgiven to Sergio Leone and Don Siegel.
Won Best Director Oscars for Unforgiven and Million Dollar Baby.

georgecukor.signature: The actor's director of classical Hollywood, with an unobtrusive camera.
georgecukor.description: Came from Broadway and let performance and dialogue lead. His comedies and literary adaptations are known above all for their female roles.

facts.text: Made ten films with Katharine Hepburn.
Was fired from Gone with the Wind a few weeks into shooting.

williamwyler.signature: The perfectionist of deep-focus staging, feared for demanding dozens of takes.
williamwyler.description: Used long takes staged in depth, so that the viewer chooses where to look, a style the critic André Bazin championed. His dramas are built on performance and moral pressure.

facts.text: Won three Best Director Oscars.
Shot The Best Years of Our Lives with Gregg Toland.

kingvidor.signature: Moved from silent social epics to fevered Technicolor melodrama.
kingvidor.description: His career ran from 1913 to 1959. The Crowd follows an ordinary clerk lost in the mass of the modern city, and his later films push emotion and landscape to extremes.

facts.text: The Crowd used hidden cameras on New York streets.
Directed the Kansas scenes of The Wizard of Oz without credit.

michaelcimino.signature: Won everything with The Deer Hunter, then made the film blamed for ending New Hollywood.
michaelcimino.description: His films stage long communal rituals, weddings, dances and hunts, before violence breaks in. His perfectionism on Heaven's Gate became a cautionary tale.

facts.text: Heaven's Gate went several times over budget and helped sink United Artists.
The Deer Hunter won Best Picture and Best Director.

straubhuillet.signature: The most uncompromising filmmakers in Europe: texts recited in landscapes, recorded in direct sound.
straubhuillet.description: A couple who worked together for five decades. They film existing texts and music with fixed shots, non-professional readers and no dubbing, refusing every form of illusion.

facts.text: Always recorded sound live on location.
In Chronicle of Anna Magdalena Bach the music is performed live on period instruments in front of the camera.

elemklimov.signature: Made what many consider the most harrowing war film ever, then never directed again.
elemklimov.description: Come and See follows a boy through the Nazi destruction of Belarusian villages, with a roaming Steadicam and faces staring into the lens.

facts.text: Come and See was his last film.
Was married to the director Larisa Shepitko and completed her last project after her death.

robertzemeckis.signature: A showman who hides ground-breaking effects inside crowd-pleasing stories.
robertzemeckis.description: A protégé of Steven Spielberg whose films are often built around a technical challenge, from mixing animation with live action to performance capture.

facts.text: Who Framed Roger Rabbit combined live action with hand-drawn animation.
Won the Best Director Oscar for Forrest Gump.

williamfriedkin.signature: Brought documentary grit to the thriller and the horror film.
williamfriedkin.description: Began in television documentary and kept its handheld immediacy. His 1970s films treat police work and demonic possession with the same unblinking realism.

facts.text: The car chase in The French Connection was shot on real Brooklyn streets.
The Exorcist was the first horror film nominated for Best Picture.

georgelucas.signature: Created Star Wars and, with it, the modern effects and franchise industry.
georgelucas.description: Started with experimental student films. His interest in sound, editing and myth produced Star Wars, and the companies he founded changed how films are made.

facts.text: Founded Industrial Light & Magic to make Star Wars.
American Graffiti is scored wall to wall with period radio hits.

stanbrakhage.signature: Made cinema a way of seeing, painting and scratching directly onto the film strip.
stanbrakhage.description: The central figure of American avant-garde film. His mostly silent films abandon story for rhythm, light and texture.

facts.text: Made close to 400 films, most of them silent.
Mothlight was made without a camera, by pressing moth wings and plants between strips of clear tape.

mikionaruse.signature: The bleakest of Japan's studio masters, chronicling women who keep going without hope.
mikionaruse.description: His films are quiet dramas about money, work and disappointment, edited with unusual briskness. He is often named alongside Ozu, Mizoguchi and Kurosawa as the fourth master of classical Japanese cinema.

facts.text: Made close to ninety films.
Frequently adapted the novelist Fumiko Hayashi and cast Hideko Takamine.

sergeiparajanov.signature: Composed films as living icons and folk tapestries.
sergeiparajanov.description: An Armenian born in Georgia who worked in Ukraine. After Shadows of Forgotten Ancestors he abandoned realism for frontal tableaux of costume, ritual and objects.

facts.text: Was imprisoned by the Soviet authorities in the 1970s.
The Colour of Pomegranates tells a poet's life through tableaux instead of scenes.

michaelmann.signature: The stylist of professional men, night cities and cool blue light.
michaelmann.description: His crime films study experts at work, cops and thieves who mirror each other. He researches procedures in detail and shoots cities at night as glowing abstractions.

facts.text: Heat put Al Pacino and Robert De Niro in a scene together for the first time.
Was an early adopter of digital cameras for night photography, in Collateral.

mauricepialat.signature: The harshest realist of French cinema, who cut scenes off before they resolved.
mauricepialat.description: A painter who came late to film. He provoked his actors toward unguarded moments and edited around the raw result, leaving gaps where other films explain.

facts.text: Trained as a painter.
Booed at Cannes when Under the Sun of Satan won the Palme d'Or, he told the crowd he did not like them either.

michaelsnow.signature: Made the camera's own movements the subject of his films.
michaelsnow.description: A Canadian painter, sculptor and musician. His structural films each explore one camera operation, a zoom, a pan, a rotation, pushed to its limit.

facts.text: Wavelength is a 45-minute zoom across a New York loft.
For La Région centrale he had a machine built to swing the camera in every direction over a mountain landscape.

bobfosse.signature: A choreographer who cut film the way he staged dance: sharp, angular and cynical.
bobfosse.description: He reinvented the film musical for a disillusioned era by confining the numbers to the stage and cutting them against the story.

facts.text: In 1973 he won an Oscar, a Tony and an Emmy for directing.
All That Jazz is a thinly veiled self-portrait.

charlesburnett.signature: Filmed Black working-class life in Los Angeles with a tenderness American cinema had not shown it.
charlesburnett.description: Part of the group of UCLA film students later called the L.A. Rebellion. Killer of Sheep observes a slaughterhouse worker and his neighbourhood in loose, plotless episodes.

facts.text: Killer of Sheep was his UCLA thesis film.
It went without a proper release for decades because of music rights.

halashby.signature: The gentle counterculture voice of 1970s Hollywood.
halashby.description: A former editor who made seven films in the 1970s about misfits and dropouts. His style is relaxed and observational, carried by pop songs.

facts.text: Won an Oscar as an editor before directing.
Harold and Maude is scored with Cat Stevens songs.

peterweir.signature: Makes films about outsiders entering closed worlds, with an undertow of mystery.
peterweir.description: A leading figure of the Australian New Wave who moved to Hollywood in the 1980s. His films set a rational outsider against a community or landscape that cannot be explained.

facts.text: Picnic at Hanging Rock helped put the Australian New Wave on the map.
The Truman Show imagined a whole life broadcast as television.

robreiner.signature: Had a run of beloved films in a different genre each time.
robreiner.description: An actor turned director whose 1980s films range from mock documentary to fairy tale, courtroom drama and romantic comedy.

facts.text: This Is Spinal Tap popularised the mock documentary and was largely improvised.
Son of the comedian and director Carl Reiner.

djibrildiopmambety.signature: Brought the freewheeling energy of the New Wave to Dakar.
djibrildiopmambety.description: A self-taught Senegalese filmmaker. His films are fragmented, musical and satirical, far from the social realism of his contemporaries.

facts.text: Made only two features, nearly twenty years apart.
Touki Bouki follows two lovers dreaming of escape to Paris.
His niece Mati Diop is also a director.

terrygilliam.signature: Builds cluttered dystopias and fantasies seen through distorting wide lenses.
terrygilliam.description: The American member of Monty Python. His films pit dreamers against bureaucracies, and his productions are famous for their disasters.

facts.text: Made the cut-out animations for Monty Python.
Fought Universal publicly over the ending of Brazil.

andrzejwajda.signature: The conscience of Polish cinema across fifty years of censorship and upheaval.
andrzejwajda.description: His early war trilogy founded the Polish Film School. He kept returning to moments when Polish history forced individuals to choose.

facts.text: Received an honorary Oscar in 2000.

toddhaynes.signature: Reworks old Hollywood forms, especially the women's picture, to ask what they concealed.
toddhaynes.description: A leading figure of the New Queer Cinema of the early 1990s. His films borrow the look of earlier eras with scholarly precision.

facts.text: Far from Heaven is modelled on Douglas Sirk's melodramas.
His early film Superstar told Karen Carpenter's story with Barbie dolls.
I'm Not There has six actors play versions of Bob Dylan.

raoulwalsh.signature: The action director of classical Hollywood, all speed and outdoor energy.
raoulwalsh.description: Directed from the 1910s to the 1960s. His gangster films, westerns and war films move fast and stay close to physical action.

facts.text: Gave John Wayne his first lead, in The Big Trail.
Lost an eye in an accident and wore an eyepatch.

jeancocteau.signature: A poet who used simple camera tricks to film myths and dreams.
jeancocteau.description: Poet, novelist, playwright and painter as well as filmmaker. His films make the fantastic matter-of-fact, with reversed motion and mirrors that turn to liquid.

facts.text: Used reversed film and a vat of mercury for the mirror effects in Orpheus.
Jean Marais starred in most of his films.

alexanderdovzhenko.signature: The lyric poet of Soviet cinema, rooted in the Ukrainian countryside.
alexanderdovzhenko.description: Where Eisenstein's montage argues, his contemplates: fields, apples, faces and death held in still, hymn-like images.

facts.text: Earth is the last part of his Ukrainian trilogy.
Tarkovsky named him as a decisive influence.

mikenichols.signature: Came from improv comedy and gave 1960s Hollywood a new, anxious tone.
mikenichols.description: A Broadway director before his first film. He drew sharp comic performances and framed them in long, carefully composed takes.

facts.text: The Graduate used existing Simon & Garfunkel songs as its score.
Was half of the comedy duo Nichols and May, with Elaine May.
Won an Emmy, a Grammy, an Oscar and a Tony.

georgearomero.signature: Invented the modern zombie film and used it as social satire.
georgearomero.description: Worked outside Hollywood in Pittsburgh. Each of his Dead films uses the same premise to attack a different target, from racism to consumerism.

facts.text: Made Night of the Living Dead in Pittsburgh on a tiny budget.
It fell into the public domain because the prints lacked a copyright notice.

abelgance.signature: The most technically audacious director of the silent era.
abelgance.description: His epics use rapid cutting, superimposition and a camera freed from the tripod years before these became common.

facts.text: The finale of Napoléon is projected across three screens side by side.
Strapped cameras to horses and swung them on pendulums.

anglee.signature: Moves between languages, genres and technologies, always circling repressed feeling.
anglee.description: Born in Taiwan and trained in the United States. He has made family comedies, Jane Austen, a martial-arts epic, a western romance and effects-driven spectacles.

facts.text: Won Best Director Oscars for Brokeback Mountain and Life of Pi.
Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon became the highest-grossing foreign-language film in the United States.

ottopreminger.signature: Used long, mobile takes to stay neutral and let the audience judge.
